answer: To resist sybil clusters, an agent registry can require cryptographic proof of historical computational work before granting validation rights. An attacker cannot simply echo previous transaction signatures across cloned nodes without re-running distinct proofs. Each legitimate node acts like a secure harbor with locked collateral, whereas rogue identities attempting automated coordination fail when their synthetic traffic lacks the nuanced, non-repetitive structure demanded by the protocol—much like distinguishing authentic reasoning from a mechanically scripted sonnet.
